- [Agentic Browser Security: Can You Trust It?](https://realagentusecases.com/en/news/2026-10-06-agentic-browser-security/): The risk-surface deep-dive of browser agents — the documented attacks, not predictions: Brave's security team showed Perplexity Comet following hidden instructions planted in a Reddit comment (white-on-white text/HTML comments) to reach a user's logged-in accounts and exfiltrate one-time passwords (Aug 2025, first in Brave's agentic-browser-security series; The Register covered it same-day), and researchers hijacked OpenAI's ChatGPT Atlas within hours of its Oct 21 2025 launch via clipboard hijacking, settings-manipulation planted in a Google Doc, and invisible phishing instructions (Fortune); why the category is the worst case for prompt injection — the OWASP LLM01 structural flaw (instructions and data share one channel, no fool-proof prevention) pointed at the three-leg risk chain all at once: untrusted input (the open web), sensitive access (your live sessions), ability to act (click buy/send/submit); the vendors agree it's unsolved — OpenAI CISO Dane Stuckey called prompt injection "a frontier, unsolved security problem" and pointed to a logged-out mode, not a cure (via Simon Willison); and the rules that hold, the same read-freely/act-through-a-gate discipline as Issue #001 — keep money and identity out of the agent's reach (a separate clean browser for banking), default to logged out, put a human on anything irreversible, scope it to low stakes, treat every page as untrusted; grounded in the Brave Comet disclosure, The Register, Fortune's Atlas coverage, Simon Willison on OpenAI's CISO, OWASP LLM01, and Issue #001; the security companion to ai-browser-agents, prompt-injection, agent-security-risks, and the human-in-the-loop gate
- [AI Agent Payment Protocols: AP2 vs ACP](https://realagentusecases.com/en/news/2026-10-07-ai-agent-payment-protocols/): The protocol-layer comparison of how an AI agent is given authority to pay — the two open standards that let a charge carry tamper-proof proof of authorization without exposing your card. Google's Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), announced Sept 16 2025 with 60+ collaborators (Mastercard, PayPal, American Express, Coinbase, Adyen, Worldpay, Intuit, Salesforce, ServiceNow), built on a chain of three cryptographically signed mandates — Intent → Cart → Payment — that forms a non-repudiable audit trail, Apache-2.0 with a Python SDK (ap2-protocol.org, github google-agentic-commerce/ap2), explicitly designed as an extension of A2A and MCP; versus the Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP) co-developed by OpenAI and Stripe (Apache-2.0, agenticcommerce.dev), the leaner merchant/platform standard that already powers ChatGPT Instant Checkout for Etsy and Shopify merchants via a Shared Payment Token that initiates a charge without the agent seeing the raw card. How they differ (industry consortium vs merchant/platform, signed-mandate chain vs delegated-token + four checkout endpoints) and what they share (tokenize the card, bind every charge to an explicit authorization). The honest early-days caveat, and the site's signature line that both just encode the same rule — gate the irreversible step, the charge bound to what you authorized, as in Issue #001's draft-then-a-human-sends discipline. The fourth connection beside MCP (tools), A2A (agents), AG-UI (you); the payment-rails companion to agentic-commerce, identity-and-access, and human-in-the-loop; grounded in Google's AP2 announcement, the AP2 repo/site, the ACP site, OpenAI's Instant Checkout, and Stripe's Shared Payment Token
- [AI Agent Code Execution: Where It Runs, Safely](https://realagentusecases.com/en/news/2026-10-08-ai-agent-code-execution/): What happens when an agent writes AND runs its own code — the answer is a disposable, isolated sandbox, not your machine, and the sandbox (not the model's intent) is the safety control. Why the pattern is spreading (Anthropic's Code execution with MCP, Nov 4 2025, cut a benchmark workflow from 150,000 to 2,000 tokens / 98.7%, while warning it "requires secure execution environments, resource limits, and monitoring"); why agent-written code is untrusted by default (honest error reaching for files/network it shouldn't, plus prompt injection — OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 GenAI risk — collapsing "the agent writes the code" into "an attacker writes the code"); the isolation ladder strongest-first (microVMs with their own kernel, e.g. E2B on Firecracker; user-space kernels like gVisor intercepting syscalls; plain containers sharing the host kernel = weakest for untrusted code); the lifecycle (request env, run, return result, discard) from the open Kubernetes SIG Agent Sandbox, and managed options — AWS Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter (isolated sandbox per execution) and Claude Code's bubblewrap/Seatbelt sandbox that boundaries shell commands but explicitly not file tools/MCP/hooks; why isolation alone is insufficient — default-deny network/filesystem (Unit 42 documented a since-remediated DNS-tunneling bypass of AWS's isolation mode, so egress control is a moving target), keep credentials out of the sandbox (inject server-side, the IAM discipline), and gate the irreversible with a human; code execution as the sharpest form of tool-calling, and the cheapest safety being to not grant a capability you don't need (Issue #001's connector runs none); grounded in Anthropic's code-execution-with-MCP post, Claude Code sandbox docs, AWS AgentCore, Kubernetes SIG Agent Sandbox, E2B/Firecracker, gVisor, OWASP LLM01, Unit 42, and Issue #001; the containment companion to tool-calling, prompt-injection, identity-and-access, human-in-the-loop, and self-hosted agents
- [OpenAI AgentKit: Build on the SDK, Not the Canvas](https://realagentusecases.com/en/news/2026-10-09-openai-agentkit/): The honest read on OpenAI's AgentKit bundle (announced at DevDay Oct 6 2025) — what's in it (Agent Builder, a drag-and-drop visual canvas; ChatKit, an embeddable chat UI; a Connector Registry; an Evals suite; and the underlying Agents SDK) and the catch most roundups skip: OpenAI's own AgentKit page carries a June 3 2026 update that Agent Builder and the Evals product will no longer be available on the platform from Nov 30 2026, with users steered to the Agents SDK (code) and ChatGPT's natural-language setup (no-code); ChatKit and the Agents SDK stay. The site's signature line — build on the layer you won't have to abandon when the vendor ships the next thing: the drag-and-drop canvas proved temporary (an eight-month lifespan), the SDK is the durable primitive, which is why teams that bet on the flashiest surface stall after the demo (why-agents-fail). The Agents SDK is a deliberately thin, provider-agnostic library (Agents/Handoffs/Guardrails/Sessions/Tracing, Python + TypeScript, MCP support, tracing on by default), the same fewer-abstractions bet it makes against LangGraph and CrewAI, consistent with Anthropic's start-simplest guidance; plus the migration reality that the Agent Builder export produces Agents SDK code, not a converted graph, so plan a rebuild-and-test pass before the deadline. Grounded in OpenAI's AgentKit announcement + wind-down note, the OpenAI Agents SDK docs, VentureBeat's launch coverage, Anthropic Building Effective Agents, and Issue #001; the vendor-bundle companion to langgraph-vs-crewai, best-tools, no-code-tools, and why-agents-fail
- [Spec-Driven Development for AI Coding Agents](https://realagentusecases.com/en/news/2026-10-12-spec-driven-development-ai-agents/): The spec-first discipline for driving coding agents -- write a clear specification (what to build and why) and review it BEFORE the agent writes code, instead of ad-hoc prompting ('vibe coding') that lets the agent guess at intent and buries the reasoning in an unreviewable chat log; the spec, not the prompt history, becomes the source of truth you, your teammates, and the agent all work from. The two best-known tools from their own docs: GitHub Spec Kit (open-source toolkit; a `specify` CLI and slash commands run in order -- constitution -> specify -> plan -> tasks -> implement, with optional clarify/analyze -- each phase producing a Markdown artifact that feeds the next, templates targeting Claude Code/GitHub Copilot/Cursor/Gemini CLI and many other agents) and AWS Kiro (its agentic IDE generates three files per spec in .kiro/specs/ -- requirements.md/design.md/tasks.md, the what/how/step-list -- with requirements as user stories in EARS 'WHEN... THE SYSTEM SHALL...' notation and approval gates that have a human review requirements before a design is generated). The honest line: a spec is real work and pure overhead for a throwaway script or quick experiment, but pays off on anything that outlives the session -- a feature a teammate will read, code on a shared repo, anything you'll debug in a month; and the spec doesn't remove the human, it moves the review earlier (you approve the intent up front and still read the final diff), making the agent's work legible, not autonomous -- the same human-in-the-loop gate moved to the front of the build. Grounded in the GitHub Spec Kit docs + repo, the AWS Kiro docs, Anthropic's Building Effective Agents (clear instructions, simplest structure that works), and Issue #001 (its system prompt is itself a spec, written and reviewed before the agent touched an inbox); the methodology companion to ai-coding-agents-for-developers, claude-agent-skills, how-to-build-an-ai-agent, langgraph-vs-crewai, and the human-in-the-loop gate
